finding.title: Empty/null key with an explicit algorithm allowlist accepts forged unsigned JWTs
finding.evidence: createVerifier only validates and prepares the key inside the guard 'if (key && keyType !== function)' at line 399. For key '' or null the guard is skipped: the type check at lines 392-397 passes because typeof is string/object, but the falsy key is never rejected and never converted to a KeyObject via prepareKeyOrSecret. The caller-supplied allowedAlgorithms (for example ['HS256']) is therefore left active with no key behind it. At verification time verifyToken computes hasKey = key instanceof Buffer ? key.length : !!key (line 180), which is false for ''/null, so neither the missing-signature branch at line 182 nor the missing-key branch at line 184 fires for a token whose signature segment is empty. validateAlgorithmAndSignature then passes the allowlist test at line 134 for alg HS256 and skips the cryptographic check because line 139 is gated on a truthy signature (if (signature && !verifySignature(...))). An attacker submits header.payload. (base64url header {"alg":"HS256"}, arbitrary payload, empty third segment) and it is accepted and returned as a valid payload with no signature verification, giving full token forgery/authentication bypass. The fixed upstream code adds the exact missing guard else if (!key && keyType !== function) throw invalidKey requiring a key unless only the none algorithm is allowed; that branch is absent here, so a falsy key silently disables signature verification whenever an algorithm allowlist is configured.

review_queue.evidence: key:'' or key:null with a signing algorithm allowed reaches verifyToken with a falsy hasKey, so an empty signature segment is accepted. Confirmed by round4-jwt-verification.json; conditional on an invalid key configuration.

finding.title: Symlink-following lock acquisition truncates arbitrary attacker-chosen files
finding.evidence: UnixFileLock._acquire builds open_flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC (line 41), conditionally adds os.O_CREAT when Path(self.lock_file).exists() is False (line 42, exists() itself follows symlinks), and then calls os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, self._context.mode) (line 44) with no os.O_NOFOLLOW and no O_EXCL. The path is the untrusted lock_file the caller supplies and is passed through os.fspath in _api.BaseFileLock.__init__ without any link/ownership validation (only ensure_directory_exists is called, line 40). An attacker who can create an entry in the lock file's parent directory (e.g. a world-writable /tmp or a directory shared between accounts) plants either a symlink or a dangling symlink at the lock path pointing at a file the victim process can write. When the victim acquires the lock, the O_CREAT flag creates the link target if it is dangling and the O_TRUNC flag truncates it to zero bytes, giving the attacker an arbitrary-file truncation/overwrite primitive (integrity/DoS) against any file the victim can write. The SoftFileLock/WindowsFileLock pre-check raise_on_not_writable_file (filelock/_util.py:22) also uses os.stat, which follows symlinks, so it does not block the planted link; and the Unix backend never calls that check at all. The only guards active here are the read-only/IsADirectory checks in _util.raise_on_not_writable_file, none of which detect that the opened inode is a symlink target rather than the intended lock file, so the unsafe open remains reachable.

review_queue.evidence: os.open at line 44 follows the attacker-controlled lock path with O_TRUNC set at line 41 and no O_NOFOLLOW; same protected-file truncation root cause one line after the expected sink. Directory write access and victim write permission are prerequisites.

finding.title: Falsy key with explicit algorithm allowlist accepts forged unsigned tokens
finding.evidence: createVerifier validates the key with `keyType !== 'string' && keyType !== 'object' && keyType !== 'function'` (lines 392-397); because `typeof null === 'object'`, `key: null` passes, and `key: ''` passes as a string. The subsequent `if (key && keyType !== 'function')` (line 399) is skipped for any falsy key, so detection/conversion of the key is never performed and `allowedAlgorithms` is left as the caller-supplied allowlist. At verify time, my message flow is: attacker token `base64url({"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}).base64url({...}).` (trailing dot, empty signature) is decoded by decoder.js line 44 into `signature === ''`. In verifyToken `hasKey` is `false` for null/'' (line 180), the guard `if (hasKey && !signature)` is false and `else if (!hasKey && signature)` is false because `''` is falsy (lines 182-186), so no missing-key/missing-signature error is raised. validateAlgorithmAndSignature (line 188) then only checks `allowedAlgorithms.includes(header.alg)` (line 134) — which passes since the attacker uses an alg from the allowlist — and the signature check `if (signature && !verifySignature(...))` (line 139) is skipped because `signature` is the empty string. No cryptographic verification occurs and the arbitrary payload is returned, i.e. an attacker who only controls the token string forges a valid identity whenever the application constructs the verifier with a falsy key (e.g. an unset/empty config value yielding '' or null) plus a non-empty algorithm list; the code never rejects falsy keys except via the 'none'-only path added in later releases. PoC not executed because the packaged dependencies (mnemonist, asn1.js, ecdsa-sig-formatter) are not installed in the audit root, but the flow is fully determined by the inspected source.

review_queue.evidence: key:'' or key:null with a signing algorithm allowed reaches verifyToken with a falsy hasKey, so an empty signature segment is accepted. Confirmed by round4-jwt-verification.json; conditional on an invalid key configuration.

finding.title: Unbounded BLAKE2b key length overflows 128-byte stack buffer in monocypher
finding.evidence: blake2b() passes caller-controlled `len(key)` straight to crypto_blake2b_keyed() (line 281); the Blake2b class does the same via crypto_blake2b_keyed_init() (line 297). The C implementation (monocypher.c:544-547) copies this size into a fixed 128-byte stack buffer: `u8 key_block[128] = {0}; COPY(key_block, key, key_size);` where COPY is an unguarded byte loop. Nothing in the binding caps the key at the BLAKE2 spec maximum (64 bytes) or the buffer size (128). Input flow: attacker/app supplies e.g. `blake2b(b'msg', key=b'A'*400)` or `Blake2b(key=b'A'*400)` -> Python bytes length 400 -> C memcpy-style loop writes 400 bytes into key_block[128], overflowing saved registers/return address with attacker-controlled bytes (stack smash, potential RCE, or reliable crash). Protections absent: no `_validate_u32`, no `if len(key) > 64`, and Cython passes the raw buffer pointer without any length check.

review_queue.evidence: blake2b passes unbounded len(key) into crypto_blake2b_keyed; monocypher.c copies key_size bytes into key_block[128]. Keys >128 bytes overflow the stack. Source-verified; remote reachability is not claimed.

finding.title: Missing fixed-length validation on key/nonce/mac buffers causes out-of-bounds reads
finding.evidence: Public API functions hand caller-controlled Python objects to C routines that unconditionally read fixed-size buffers, without validating length. Examples: lock() line 181 and unlock() line 199 pass unvalidated `key` (C reads key[32]) and `nonce` (nonce[24]); unlock() additionally passes user `mac` with no length check (crypto_aead_unlock reads mac[16]) unlike IncrementalAuthenticatedEncryption.unlock() which does check (line 246); chacha20() lines 266-269 pass an unvalidated `key` even though crypto_chacha20_x/djb read key[32]; key_exchange() line 375 and compute_key_exchange_public_key() line 362 pass `their_public_key`/`secret_key` with no length check (x25519 reads 32 bytes); signature_check() line 429 passes signature/public_key with no check (reads 64 and 32 bytes). Cython coerces a bytes argument to `const uint8_t*` and passes the raw pointer with no length enforcement, so a short buffer (e.g. `unlock(b'k', b'n', b'm', b'...')`) makes Monocypher read up to 31/23/15/63 bytes past the heap object. Consequence is out-of-bounds read influencing the operation and a reachable crash (DoS) when the object sits at a page boundary.

review_queue.evidence: lock()/unlock() pass caller-controlled key and nonce buffers into native routines declaring key[32]/nonce[24] without a length check; the incremental wrapper guards lengths at lines 214-218. Distinct AEAD bounds defect; no native crash or disclosure reproduced.

finding.title: Unchecked malloc result in argon2i_32 dereferenced as NULL by crypto_argon2
finding.evidence: argon2i_32() computes `work_area = malloc((<size_t> nb_blocks) * 1024)` (line 345) and immediately calls crypto_argon2() with it (line 347) inside try/finally, without checking for NULL. `nb_blocks` is fully caller-controlled (only bounded to 32 bits by the uint32_t config assignment). Passing a large value such as 0xFFFFFFFF asks malloc for ~4 TiB; when the allocator fails and returns NULL, crypto_argon2() executes `blk *blocks = (blk*)work_area;` and writes through it (monocypher.c:757, block fills at 772-794), dereferencing NULL and crashing the process. The only protection is free(work_area) in the finally block, which does not prevent the NULL dereference; the allocation result is never validated (contrast with the explicit _validate_u32 length checks used elsewhere).

review_queue.evidence: malloc at line 345 is unchecked before crypto_argon2 consumes work_area at 347; a failed allocation dereferences NULL. Distinct availability failure from a successfully sized undersized allocation; OOM was not executed.

finding.title: UnixFileLock follows symlinks when opening the lock file, enabling arbitrary file truncation/chmod
finding.evidence: The lock file path is caller-supplied and reaches UnixFileLock._acquire (filelock/_unix.py lines 39-55). At line 41 `open_flags = os.O_RDWR | os.O_TRUNC`; line 42 checks `Path(self.lock_file).exists()` and only line 43 adds `os.O_CREAT` when it exists; line 44 calls `os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, self._context.mode)` with no `O_NOFOLLOW`, then line 46 calls `os.fchmod(fd, self._context.mode)`. Because pathlib exists()/os.stat() resolve symlinks, if an attacker with write access to the directory containing a predictable lock file (e.g. a shared world-writable temp directory such as /tmp/<app>.lock) pre-creates that path as a symlink to a victim file, the exists() probe returns True, O_CREAT is skipped, and the O_RDWR|O_TRUNC open follows the link and truncates the victim file to zero bytes; the subsequent os.fchmod then applies the lock mode (default 0o644) to the victim. The only mitigation, `with suppress(PermissionError)` around fchmod (line 45-46), does not stop the truncation already performed by open(), and unlike SoftFileLock (which uses O_EXCL) the UNIX backend never prevents link resolution, so no protection blocks this integrity violation.

review_queue.evidence: os.open at line 44 follows the attacker-controlled lock path with O_TRUNC set at line 41 and no O_NOFOLLOW; same protected-file truncation root cause one line after the expected sink. Directory write access and victim write permission are prerequisites.

finding.title: clear() is not panic-safe, letting a panicking element Drop cause a double-free
finding.evidence: `ThinVec::clear` (line 1082) runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` at line 1084 and only afterwards resets the length with `self.set_len(0)` at line 1085. There is no guard to run `set_len(0)` during unwinding. If any element's `Drop` panics, `drop_in_place` unwinds out of `clear` before line 1085 executes, so `self.header().len()` still reports the old length even though those elements were already dropped. The `ThinVec` remains owned by the caller (no unsafe is required to trigger this, a panicking destructor is ordinary safe Rust), and the `Drain`/leak-amplification comments elsewhere in the file show the intended invariant is that length must be repaired on every path. On the next `clear`, `drop`, `truncate` or `Drain::drop`, the already-freed elements are dropped a second time, producing a double free / use-after-free. A local PoC built against this crate (path dependency, default features) confirmed it: with element 1 panicking during `clear`, output was `CLEAR panicked=true len_after_clear=3` and `CLEAR drops per element (sound=[1,1,1]) = [2, 2, 2]`, i.e. every element's destructor ran twice through safe code.

review_queue.evidence: clear drops its slice at 1084 before setting len to zero at 1085, so a destructor panic leaves a stale live length that a later drop re-drops. reference/FIX.md independently patches this path; distinct from IntoIter cleanup.

finding.title: IntoIter::drop is not panic-safe, double-dropping already-consumed/moved elements
finding.evidence: `IntoIter::drop` calls the helper `drop_non_singleton` (line 2544), which at line 2546 moves the backing `ThinVec` into a local with `mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new())`, then at line 2547 runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` and at line 2548 resets the length with `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)`. The reset only executes if the drop loop completes. If an element in `[start..]` panics in its `Drop`, line 2548 is skipped and the local `vec` is itself dropped while unwinding, invoking `ThinVec::drop` with its original (un-shortened) length, so all elements are dropped again. Moreover, elements before `start` were already moved out by `Iterator::next` (`ptr::read` at line 2510) without reducing the header length, so the unwind drops values that have been moved out of the vector, corrupting ownership. No unsafe code is needed by the caller: a normal panicking destructor suffices. A local PoC built against this crate confirmed it: after `it.next()` moved element 0 out and element 1 panicked during `drop(it)`, output was `INTO_ITER panicked=true first_is_some=true` and `INTO_ITER drops per element (sound=[0,1,1]) = [1, 2, 2]`, i.e. the moved-out element 0 was dropped once more and elements 1 and 2 were each dropped twice.

review_queue.evidence: IntoIter::drop drops its tail before zeroing len, so a destructor panic drops the stale local vector again. Same expected root cause at the adjacent unsafe operation.

finding.title: Unbounded BLAKE2b key length overflows 128-byte stack buffer in crypto_blake2b_keyed_init
finding.evidence: blake2b(msg, key=None) never validates len(key); it forwards the raw attacker-controlled length to crypto_blake2b_keyed(hash, 64, key, len(key), msg, len(msg)) (line 281, and the same sink is reached from Blake2b.__init__ at line 297). In monocypher.c the callee does `u8 key_block[128] = {0}; COPY(key_block, key, key_size);` (monocypher.c:530-549, COPY macro at monocypher.c:65 expands to `for(_i_,0,size) dst[_i_]=src[_i_]`). With key_size==len(key)>128 the loop writes key[0..key_size-1] into the 128-byte stack array, corrupting the stack (return address/adjacent locals). The C library documents key_size<=64 but performs no bound check, and the binding supplies no check either, so a caller passing e.g. key=b'A'*1000 (attacker-controlled input to the crypto wrapper) drives a fully controlled-length stack overflow write. Reproduced by inspection of the compiled-in monocypher.c source; no compiler is available in this environment to run the C-level PoC.

review_queue.evidence: blake2b passes unbounded len(key) into crypto_blake2b_keyed; monocypher.c copies key_size bytes into key_block[128]. Keys >128 bytes overflow the stack. Source-verified; remote reachability is not claimed.

finding.title: Unvalidated argon2i nb_blocks causes heap overflow and out-of-bounds read
finding.evidence: argon2i_32 copies nb_blocks verbatim into config.nb_blocks (line 328) without the _validate_u32 guard used for the password/salt/key/ad sizes, then allocates work_area = malloc(nb_blocks * 1024) (line 345) and calls crypto_argon2(..., work_area, ...) (line 347). For an attacker-chosen nb_blocks=1, monocypher.c:752-757 computes segment_size = 1/1/4 = 0 and lane_size = 0 (C nb_blocks becomes 0), yet the per-lane init loop `FOR_T(u32,i,0,2) ... load64_le_buf(blocks[l*lane_size+i].a, hash_area, 128)` (monocypher.c:777-781) writes both blocks[0] and blocks[1] = 2048 bytes into a 1024-byte allocation, a heap buffer overflow. It then sets `blk *last_block = blocks + lane_size - 1` = blocks-1 (monocypher.c:908) and serializes blocks[-1] into the returned 32-byte hash (monocypher.c:911-919), leaking 1024 bytes of adjacent heap data back to the caller via an out-of-bounds read. Monocypher requires nb_blocks >= 8*nb_lanes; the binding never enforces this, so nb_blocks values 1..3 (and huge values that make malloc return NULL, which is also unchecked and then dereferenced) are all reachable from untrusted input. Verified by source inspection; environment lacks a C compiler to execute the PoC.

review_queue.evidence: crypto_argon2 is called with the caller-sized work area; same undersized-work-area root cause as the expected line-345 sink.

finding.title: Double free in ThinVec::clear() when an element destructor panics
finding.evidence: Reachable from safe Rust: hold a `ThinVec<T>` whose element type `T` has a panicking `Drop` and call `clear()` (line 1082). `clear` runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` (line 1084) and only afterwards `self.set_len(0)` (line 1085). The slice drop glue is panic-safe: even if the destructor of one element panics, it drops all remaining elements before propagating the unwind. Because the length is still the original value, the panic skips line 1085, and as the `ThinVec` is dropped during unwinding, `ThinVec::drop` -> `drop_non_singleton` runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` (line 1917) with the stale length, dropping every element a second time -> double free / use-after-free. No guard resets the length before the fallible drop; upstream 0.2.16 fixed this exact bug with a DropGuard that zeroes the length on unwind (RELEASES.md: "Fix two double-drop issues with ThinVec::clear() and ThinVec::into_iter() when the Drop implementation of the item panics").

review_queue.evidence: clear drops its slice at 1084 before setting len to zero at 1085, so a destructor panic leaves a stale live length that a later drop re-drops. reference/FIX.md independently patches this path; distinct from IntoIter cleanup.

finding.title: Double free in IntoIter drop when a remaining element destructor panics
finding.evidence: Reachable from safe Rust: obtain a `ThinVec<T>` whose element type `T` has a panicking `Drop`, call `into_iter()`, consume some elements, then let the iterator fall out of scope while a not-yet-yielded element's destructor panics. `IntoIter::drop` (line 2539) calls `drop_non_singleton` (line 2544), which moves the vector out with `mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new())` (line 2546) and then runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` (line 2547). If a destructor panics, the slice drop glue still drops the remaining elements, and line 2548 `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` is skipped. The local `vec` is then dropped while unwinding with its original length (which also covers the already-yielded prefix that was moved out by `next()`), so `ThinVec::drop` re-drops already-moved-out and already-dropped elements -> double free / use-after-free. The length is not cleared before the fallible drop; upstream 0.2.16 replaced this with a DropGuard that sets the length to 0 during unwind.

review_queue.evidence: IntoIter::drop drops its tail before zeroing len, so a destructor panic drops the stale local vector again. Same expected root cause at the adjacent unsafe operation.

finding.title: Symlink-following lock open with O_TRUNC truncates arbitrary files
finding.evidence: UnixFileLock._acquire (filelock/_unix.py) builds open_flags including os.O_TRUNC at line 41, and for an already-existing lock path calls os.open(self.lock_file, open_flags, self._context.mode) at line 44. The open follows symbolic links (no O_NOFOLLOW and no lstat()/S_ISREG check) and is opened with O_TRUNC, unlike SoftFileLock which uses O_CREAT|O_EXCL and therefore refuses to act on a pre-existing path. The pre-check at line 42 (Path(self.lock_file).exists()) also resolves symlinks and therefore cannot detect or block the link, and UnixFileLock never calls raise_on_not_writable_file() the way _soft.py (line 17) and _windows.py (line 20) do. Input flow: the lock_file path is caller/attacker-influenced (e.g. a predictable name derived from a filename or placed in a world-writable directory such as /tmp); a local attacker with write access to that directory pre-creates the path as a symlink to a victim-owned file. When the victim process calls acquire(), os.open resolves the symlink and O_TRUNC zeroes the target file, destroying its contents (integrity/availability loss, arbitrary file clobber). The only configuration needed is that the lock path is attacker-controllable or resides in an attacker-writable directory; the same path through SoftFileLock would fail safely with EEXIST. The libc flock() call at line 48 occurs after truncation, so it does not prevent the write.

review_queue.evidence: os.open at line 44 follows the attacker-controlled lock path with O_TRUNC set at line 41 and no O_NOFOLLOW; same protected-file truncation root cause one line after the expected sink. Directory write access and victim write permission are prerequisites.

finding.title: Unconstrained paddedInLength/inBlockIndex lets prover force bogus SHA256 output via out-of-range ItemAtIndex index
finding.evidence: The prover-controlled input `paddedInLength` is never range-checked with a bit decomposition; it is only constrained by `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9); paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512` (lines 110-111, duplicated at 233-234) and by `bitLengthVerifier = LessEqThan(maxBitsPaddedBits); bitLengthVerifier.in[0] <== paddedInLength; bitLengthVerifier.in[1] <== maxBitLength; bitLengthVerifier.out === 1` (lines 125-128, duplicated at 237-240). circomlib's LessThan/LessEqThan is sound only when both operands are below 2^n; it runs Num2Bits(n+1) on `in[0]+2^n-in[1]`, which is reduced mod p. Setting `paddedInLength = p-1` makes the reduced value small (e.g. 510 for maxBitLength=512), so `bitLengthVerifier.out === 1` is satisfied even though paddedInLength hugely exceeds maxBitLength. That makes `inBlockIndex = paddedInLength/512 mod p` arbitrary, so `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1` (line 195, and line 292 in Sha256Partial) becomes an arbitrary field element. The matching guard in ItemAtIndex (array.circom lines 25-28) uses the same under-constrained LessThan, so an index such as p-1 or any value >= maxBlocks passes `lessThan.out === 1`. Since no `eqs[i]` then matches, CalculateTotal sums to 0 and every `out[k]` is forced to 0, letting a prover generate an accepted witness whose SHA256 output is 0 for a declared length outside the intended domain. The circuit therefore fails to enforce paddedInLength <= maxBitLength and 1 <= inBlockIndex <= maxBlocks (valid in-range index), defeating the intended validation.

review_queue.evidence: bitLengthVerifier connection for the unbounded paddedInLength; same comparator/length root cause.

finding.title: SHA-256 circuit does not bind prover-chosen length to message padding, allowing intermediate/prefix hash attestation
finding.evidence: Attacker-controlled inputs are `paddedIn[maxBitLength]` (line 96) and `paddedInLength` (line 97). At line 110 `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9)` and line 111 `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512` constrain only that `paddedInLength` is a 512-bit multiple up to `maxBitLength` (checked by the verifier at lines 125-128); nothing constrains the content of `paddedIn` to contain valid SHA-256 padding (the 0x80 byte and the 64-bit length suffix), and the intended floor/padding verifiers are commented out (lines 114-122). The attacker-chosen `inBlockIndex` flows directly into `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1` (line 195) and selects `sha256compression[inBlockIndex-1].out` as the public output `out` (line 196), so the circuit returns the chaining value after an arbitrary block boundary rather than the final digest. Concretely, with the same `paddedIn` bytes the prover can set `paddedInLength` to select the state after block 0, making `out` the SHA-256 compression state of a prefix (e.g. the first 64 bytes) instead of SHA256 of the claimed message. The check at lines 125-128 only bounds the magnitude of the length, so the digest is not cryptographically bound to a specific padded message; any consumer that treats `out` as SHA256 of `paddedIn` (e.g. DKIM body-hash matching in ZK Email) receives a value the prover can choose to be an unauthenticated intermediate block state, breaking the binding the circuit is intended to provide.

review_queue.evidence: Unbounded inBlockIndex derivation; same comparator/length root cause as the expected sink.

finding.title: Public/private key misdetection enables HS256 algorithm-confusion token forgery
finding.evidence: Input: an application configures the verifier with a public key (e.g. an RSA SPKI PEM) whose string is not matched by the anchored regex, such as when the PEM text is prefixed by a leading newline/whitespace (a common artifact of reading keys from .env/env vars/templates). Flow: createVerifier calls detectPublicKeyAlgorithms(key) at src/verifier.js:401 (and src/verifier.js:342 for async key callbacks). In src/crypto.js performDetectPublicKeyAlgorithms (lines 125-136), the only public-key test is key.match(/^-----BEGIN(?: (RSA))? PUBLIC KEY-----/); unlike performDetectPrivateKeyAlgorithm (src/crypto.js:78) which does key.trim().match(...), this path never trims. A leading-whitespace PEM therefore fails publicKeyPemMatch and does not include '-----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----', so the branch at line 133 falls through and returns hsAlgorithms. Consequently src/verifier.js:409 executes prepareKeyOrSecret(key, 'HS256' === hsAlgorithms[0]) => true, creating an HMAC secret (createSecretKey) from the PEM text, and the allowlist at src/verifier.js:404/347 becomes the shared-secret hsAlgorithms. Failed protection: validateAlgorithmAndSignature (src/verifier.js:134) now accepts header.alg 'HS256', and verifySignature's HS branch (src/crypto.js:284) recomputes HMAC-SHA256 over the same input using the same key material. Because a verification public key is not secret, an attacker who knows it can HMAC-sign an arbitrary token with the exact PEM string as the key and the forgery validates. Demonstrated locally: createVerifier({ key: '\n' + rsaPublicKeyPem })(HS256 token signed with that same '\n'+PEM string) returned {"sub":"attacker","role":"admin"}, whereas the identical key without the leading newline was rejected with FAST_JWT_INVALID_ALGORITHM (asymmetric detection worked).

review_queue.evidence: Claimed HS256 algorithm confusion when PEM key material is not matched at offset 0. The detection path and a working forgery were not reproduced; keep unreviewed.

finding.title: ThinVec::clear double-drops elements when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: clear() (line 1082) runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` at line 1084) over the whole logical slice and only afterwards calls `self.set_len(0)` (line 1085). Unlike `truncate`, which deliberately decrements the length before each `drop_in_place` (lines 1059-1063), clear drops every element while `len` is still the original length. If any element's destructor panics (a safe, supported operation: e.g. a user type whose Drop panics, or shared data that panics), `set_len(0)` is skipped and unwinding begins with the vector still reporting the old `len`. The unwind then drops the `ThinVec` itself, whose `Drop` impl calls `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])` again (line 1917) over the same range, re-dropping elements that were already destroyed -> double free / use-after-free and potential heap corruption. No special configuration is required (default features). Upstream confirmed this as a real defect and fixed it in 0.2.16 (RELEASES.md: "Fix two double-drop issues with ThinVec::clear() and ThinVec::into_iter() when the Drop implementation of the item panics"); the 0.2.21 code wraps the slice in a DropGuard that sets len to 0 on unwind, while this 0.2.15 target has no guard.

review_queue.evidence: clear drops its slice at 1084 before setting len to zero at 1085, so a destructor panic leaves a stale live length that a later drop re-drops. reference/FIX.md independently patches this path; distinct from IntoIter cleanup.

finding.title: IntoIter::drop double-drops elements when an element's Drop panics
finding.evidence: `Drop for IntoIter<T>` (line 2539) calls drop_non_singleton, which moves the vector out with `mem::replace(&mut this.vec, ThinVec::new())`, runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` (line 2547), and only then calls `vec.set_len_non_singleton(0)` (line 2548). If any destructor invoked at line 2547 panics, the trailing `set_len_non_singleton(0)` never executes, and the local `vec` is dropped during unwinding. Its `Drop for ThinVec` (line 1917) re-runs `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[..])` using the still-unchanged `len`, which not only re-drops the partially destroyed tail (`start..len`) but also drops the range `0..start` whose elements were already moved out by earlier `IntoIter::next` calls -> double free / use-after-free. Reachable from safe code whenever a `ThinVec<T>` is consumed via `into_iter()` and `T::drop` panics (no special features needed). This is the second defect fixed upstream in 0.2.16; the 0.2.21 implementation installs a DropGuard that zeroes the length on unwind before dropping, which is absent here.

review_queue.evidence: IntoIter::drop drops its tail before zeroing len, so a destructor panic drops the stale local vector again. Same expected root cause at the adjacent unsafe operation.

finding.title: Double free when an element's destructor panics during ThinVec::clear()
finding.evidence: ThinVec::clear() drops the live elements via `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut self[..])` (line 1084) while the header length still holds the old length, and only resets it with `self.set_len(0)` on line 1085 after the drop loop returns. Attacker-reachable input is any safe code holding a `ThinVec<T>` where `T::drop` may panic (e.g. a value whose Drop impl panics, or a nested container whose member destructor unwinds). If any element's destructor panics, unwinding skips line 1085, so the stored length is left unchanged while the slice drop glue has already dropped every element exactly once (std's drop glue drops the remaining elements on unwind). When the vector is later dropped, `impl Drop for ThinVec` (line 1917, `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut this[..])`) re-runs over the same non-zero length and drops all elements a second time, producing a double free / use-after-free of any heap-owning element. There is no drop guard resetting the length before/while dropping, which is precisely the protection later upstream versions add. Reproduced locally with tests/poc.rs: the control path (no panicking destructor) performs 3 drops for 3 elements and passes, while the panicking-destructor path reports `DOUBLE DROP: 3 elements produced 6 Drop invocations (double free)` (assert left: 6, right: 3). The same unguarded pattern exists in `impl Drop for IntoIter` at lines 2546-2548, where a panic inside `ptr::drop_in_place(&mut vec[this.start..])` skips `set_len_non_singleton(0)` and the temporary `vec` is then dropped with its stale length, double-dropping the whole buffer.

review_queue.evidence: clear drops its slice at 1084 before setting len to zero at 1085, so a destructor panic leaves a stale live length that a later drop re-drops. reference/FIX.md independently patches this path; distinct from IntoIter cleanup.

finding.title: Unbounded Blake2b key length causes stack buffer overflow
finding.evidence: Blake2b.__init__ (line 294-297) accepts an arbitrary-length key and passes len(key) directly as the key_size argument of crypto_blake2b_keyed_init, with no upper-bound check (the class docstring even suggests 'the optional 32-byte key' but nothing enforces it). In monocypher.c:530-546 crypto_blake2b_keyed_init declares a 128-byte stack buffer `u8 key_block[128]` and then executes COPY(key_block, key, key_size), where COPY is a plain element-by-element copy loop (monocypher.c:65). A caller supplying a key longer than 128 bytes (e.g. moncohypher.Blake2b(key=b'A'*200) or the module-level blake2b(msg, key) at line 281 which calls crypto_blake2b_keyed) overwrites the stack past key_block, giving attacker-controlled memory corruption. The only protection would be a key_size <= 64 check and it is absent.

review_queue.evidence: Blake2b.__init__ passes unbounded len(key) into crypto_blake2b_keyed_init, the same fixed key_block[128] copy as line 281. Genuine separate wrapper defect from the expected argon2 undersized work area.

finding.title: Missing length validation of signature/public_key in signature_check
finding.evidence: signature_check(signature, public_key, message) forwards attacker-supplied peer data straight to crypto_eddsa_check without verifying len(signature)==64 or len(public_key)==32 (lines 419-429; the C declaration at line 111 expects uint8_t signature[64] and public_key[32]). The C routine reads all 64 signature bytes and 32 public-key bytes; if a protocol peer sends a shorter signature or public key, the reads run past the end of the Python bytes buffer (out-of-bounds read) and can crash the interpreter. Every other keyed entry point either validates (IncrementalAuthenticatedEncryption, elligator_*) or documents the size, but here the untrusted input path has no bounds check.

review_queue.evidence: signature_check forwards caller-controlled signature and public key to crypto_eddsa_check, which reads fixed-size signature[64]/public_key[32] without a wrapper length check. Source-verified wrapper bounds defect.

finding.title: Unvalidated BLAKE2b key length causes stack buffer overflow in monocypher
finding.evidence: blake2b() forwards a caller-supplied key of arbitrary length straight into the C library: line 281 calls crypto_blake2b_keyed(hash, len(hash), key, len(key), msg, len(msg)) and the Blake2b class does the same at line 297 (crypto_blake2b_keyed_init(&self._ctx, self._hash_size, key, len(key))). No key-length check exists in the binding (contrast the explicit length checks in elligator_map/elligator_rev/elligator_key_pair and the AEAD class). monocypher.c:544-546 implements the sink as 'u8 key_block[128] = {0}; COPY(key_block, key, key_size);' where COPY is an unbounded byte loop ('#define COPY(dst, src, size) FOR(_i_, 0, size) (dst)[_i_] = (src)[_i_]', monocypher.c:65). key_size = len(key), so any attacker-controlled key longer than 128 bytes writes that many bytes into the 128-byte stack buffer, corrupting the stack with attacker-chosen data. Reachable purely from Python, e.g. blake2b(b'x', key=b'A'*200) or Blake2b(key=b'A'*200); the key is typically a secret/derived value supplied by the application, making this a stack memory-corruption primitive.

review_queue.evidence: blake2b passes unbounded len(key) into crypto_blake2b_keyed; monocypher.c copies key_size bytes into key_block[128]. Keys >128 bytes overflow the stack. Source-verified; remote reachability is not claimed.

finding.title: Module-level crypto wrappers pass unvalidated caller buffers to fixed-size C reads
finding.evidence: signature_check() (line 429) calls crypto_eddsa_check(signature, public_key, message, len(message)) without validating that signature is 64 bytes and public_key is 32 bytes. The C callee unconditionally reads signature[64] and public_key[32] (monocypher.c crypto_eddsa_check -> crypto_eddsa_check_equation, which does load32_le_buf(s32, s, 8) with s = signature+32 and calls ge_frombytes_neg_vartime on public_key). Cython converts the Python bytes objects to raw pointers (e.g. PyBytes_AS_STRING) with no length enforcement, so a signature or public_key shorter than the expected size causes reads past the end of the heap buffer. The same omission exists in unlock() at line 199 (crypto_aead_unlock reads mac[16], key[32], nonce[24] from caller-supplied bytes), key_exchange() line 375 (reads secret[32]/public[32]) and compute_key_exchange_public_key() line 362, while the IncrementalAuthenticatedEncryption class (lines 246-247) and the elligator_* functions do validate lengths - showing the checks are expected but missing on these module-level paths.

review_queue.evidence: signature_check forwards caller-controlled signature and public key to crypto_eddsa_check, which reads fixed-size signature[64]/public_key[32] without a wrapper length check. Source-verified wrapper bounds defect.

finding.title: Under-constrained block index/length in Sha256General lets prover pick which SHA-256 compression block becomes the output
finding.evidence: In `Sha256General` (and identically `Sha256Partial`, line 233) the block index used to select the returned digest is derived from the attacker-supplied `paddedInLength` with the non-deterministic assignment `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9)` (line 110). The only binding constraint is `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512` (line 111). Because 512 is invertible in the BN254 scalar field, this equation is satisfiable for ANY field element `paddedInLength` — the prover simply sets `inBlockIndex = paddedInLength * 512^-1 mod p` — so it does not enforce that `paddedInLength` is an integer multiple of 512 nor that `inBlockIndex` equals the integer floor of `paddedInLength/512`. The integer-domain floor checks that were written to guarantee this (`floorVerifierUnder`/`floorVerifierOver`, lines 114-122) are commented out and thus never emitted as constraints; the only remaining length check is `bitLengthVerifier = LessEqThan(maxBitsPaddedBits)` (lines 125-128), which merely bounds the top of `paddedInLength`. The unchecked `inBlockIndex` then directly drives the output multiplexer `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1` (line 195), choosing which of the `maxBlocks` pre-computed `sha256compression[i].out[k]` states becomes the public `out[k]`. A malicious prover can therefore choose `inBlockIndex` (equivalently `paddedInLength`) to make the circuit attest to the intermediate hash after an arbitrary number of blocks rather than the hash of the correctly padded, full message, decoupling `out` from the message/length the verifier believes was hashed. This is compounded by the fact that the contents of `paddedIn` are never checked against `paddedInLength` (padding/zero-tail check explicitly abandoned in the comment at lines 130-131), so no constraint ties the claimed length/index to the actual message bits. A verifier that consumes `out` as the SHA-256 of a specific message cannot distinguish such a proof, breaking the circuit's soundness/integrity guarantee.

review_queue.evidence: Unbounded inBlockIndex derivation; same comparator/length root cause as the expected sink.

finding.title: SHA-256 circuit does not validate padding/message length, allowing prover-chosen message-boundary and length-extension forgeries
finding.evidence: Attacker input: the prover supplies the untrusted witness signals `paddedIn[maxBitLength]` (line 96) and `paddedInLength` (line 97); both flow into `Sha256General` via `Sha256Bytes` (sha.paddedIn[i*8+j] <== bytes[i].out[7-j], line 30; sha.paddedInLength <== paddedInLength*8, line 33) or via `Sha256BytesPartial` (lines 62/65). Flow: `paddedInLength` drives `inBlockIndex <-- (paddedInLength >> 9)` (line 110) and the only binding condition is `paddedInLength === inBlockIndex * 512` (line 111) plus `LessEqThan` `paddedInLength <= maxBitLength` (lines 125-128). Unsafe operation: `out[k]` is taken from the compression output selected by the prover-chosen index `arraySelectors[k].index <== inBlockIndex - 1` (line 195, mirrored at line 292), and `sha256compression[i].inp[k] <== paddedIn[i*512+k]` (line 184) feeds raw attacker bytes into the compression. Failed protection: there is no constraint that `paddedIn` is a valid SHA-256 padding (no 0x80 terminator check, no zero-fill check, no 64-bit message-length-field check) and no constraint tying `paddedInLength` to the real message length; the floor/padding verifiers are commented out (lines 114-122) and the source itself states padding verification is deferred 'outside the circuit' (lines 130-131). Consequence: a malicious prover can choose the block boundary and the trailing padding/length bytes arbitrarily, so `out` is the chaining value of an attacker-chosen prefix/suffix rather than a commitment to the exact message. This lets a prover present the same/first message bytes with a different declared length and append additional blocks (length extension), breaking any surrounding protocol that treats the circuit output as SHA-256 of the supplied message (e.g. header/body hashing in email-verifier.circom lines 67 and 136). The only effective mitigation present (`assert(2 ** maxBitsPaddedBits > maxBitLength)`, lines 92/215) bounds the length comparison but does not validate padding or bind the output to the intended message.

review_queue.evidence: sha.circom:130-131 explicitly delegates padding to callers; selecting the declared prefix is the component interface. Same reasoning as the round-4 review, not a demonstrated caller violation.
